\\section{Preliminaries}\\label{sec:prelim}

\\begin{definition}
A \\emph{hyperfield} is a set "'$'"\\Hb"'$ with a distinguished element $0$, a
multiplication making $'"\\Hb"'^'"\\times:=\\Hb\\setminus\\{0\\}"'$ an abelian group
(with $0'"\\cdot a=0"'$ for all $a$), the notation $-a:=(-1)a$, and a
hyperaddition $'"\\bp:\\Hb\\times\\Hb\\to\\mathcal P(\\Hb)\\setminus\\{\\varnothing\\}"'$
satisfying:
'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=(H\\arabic*)]
\\item "'$x'"\\bp y=y\\bp x"'$;'"\\; "'$x'"\\bp0=\\{x\\}"'$;'"\\; "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\iff y=-x"'$;
'"\\item "'$(x'"\\bp y)\\bp z=x\\bp(y\\bp z)"'$, where for $S'"\\subseteq\\Hb"'$,
$S'"\\bp z:=\\bigcup_{s\\in S}s\\bp z"'$. All bracketings of an iterated sum
coincide; we write $x_1'"\\bp\\cdots\\bp x_n"'$ and denote by $a''^{'"\\bp k}"'$ the
$k$-fold hypersum of $a$ with itself;
'"\\item "'$a(x'"\\bp y)\\subseteq ax\\bp ay"'$ (weak distributivity);
'"\\item "'$t'"\\in x\\bp y\\implies x\\in t\\bp(-y)"'$ (reversibility).
'"\\end{enumerate}
These are the hyperfields of Krasner, in the form used by Baker and Bowler
for matroids (they impose "'$a(x'"\\bp y)=ax\\bp ay"'$ outright; by
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i) this follows from (H3)).
\\end{definition}

\\begin{lemma}[elementary consequences]\\label{lem:basic}
Let "'$a,x,y,z'"\\in\\Hb"'$, $a'"\\neq0"'$.
'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(\\roman*)}]
\\item "'$a(x'"\\bp y)=ax\\bp ay"'$;
'"\\item "'$-(x'"\\bp y)=(-x)\\bp(-y)"'$;
'"\\item "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z\\iff -z\\in x\\bp y"'$;
'"\\item if "'$x'"\\bp y=\\{t\\}"'$ is a singleton with $x,y'"\\neq0"'$, then
$-y'"\\in x\\bp(-t)"'$ and $-x'"\\in y\\bp(-t)"'$;
'"\\item if "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ then $0'"\\in(ax)\\bp(ay)\\bp(az)"'$.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
(i) (H3) gives "'$'"\\subseteq"'$; (H3) with scalar $a''^{-1}$ gives
$a''^{-1}(ax'"\\bp ay)\\subseteq x\\bp y"'$, i.e.'"\\ "'$'"\\supseteq"'$.
(ii) is (i) with $a=-1$.
(iii) If $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ then $0'"\\in t\\bp z"'$ for some $t'"\\in x\\bp y"'$,
whence $z=-t'"\\in-(x\\bp y)"'$ by (H1), i.e.'"\\ "'$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ by (ii).
Conversely $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ gives
$0'"\\in(-z)\\bp z\\subseteq x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ by (H1).
(iv) From $t'"\\in x\\bp y"'$, (H4) gives $x'"\\in t\\bp(-y)"'$, i.e.'"\\
"'$0'"\\in t\\bp(-y)\\bp(-x)"'$ by (H1) applied to the pair $'"\\{t\\bp(-y)\\},\\{-x\\}"'$:
precisely, $x'"\\in t\\bp(-y)"'$ means $0'"\\in(t\\bp(-y))\\bp(-x)"'$ using (H1) in the
form $0'"\\in u\\bp v\\iff v=-u"'$. Then $-t'"\\in(-y)\\bp(-x)=-(x\\bp y)=\\{-t\\}"'$
(Lemma (ii)), i.e.'"\\ the singleton "'$'"\\{-t\\}"'$ equals the set $(-x)'"\\bp(-y)"'$
'"\\emph{as far as the element "'$-t$ is concerned}: we have shown
$-t'"\\in(-x)\\bp(-y)"'$, so by (H4) $-y'"\\in(-t)\\bp x=x\\bp(-t)"'$. The second
membership is symmetric.
(v) From $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ (part (iii)) and (i),
$-'"\\lambda z\\in\\lambda x\\bp\\lambda y"'$, hence (iii) again.
'"\\end{proof}

For a finite multiset "'$M$ of elements of $'"\\Hb"'$ we write $'"\\boxplus M"'$ for the
unambiguous hypersum of its elements.

'"\\begin{lemma}[substitution atoms]\\label{lem:atoms}
Let "'$a,b,c'"\\in\\Hb"'^{'"\\times}"'$ with $-c'"\\in a\\bp b"'$.
'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(A\\arabic*)}]
\\item "'$0'"\\in a\\bp b\\bp c"'$ and, for every $k'"\\ge1"'$,
$0'"\\in a"'^{'"\\bp k}\\bp b"'^{'"\\bp k}\\bp c"'^{'"\\bp k}"'$.
'"\\item \\textup{(cubing a pair sum)} With
"'$(a'"\\bp b)"'^{'"\\cdot3}:=\\{t_1t_2t_3:t_i\\in a\\bp b\\}"'$,
'"\\[
  -c"'^{3}'"\\ \\in\\ (a\\bp b)"'^{'"\\cdot3}\\ \\subseteq\\
   a"'^{3}'"\\bp\\bigl(a"'^{2}b'"\\bigr)"'^{'"\\bp3}\\bp\\bigl(ab"'^{2}'"\\bigr)"'^{'"\\bp3}\\bp b"'^{3}.
'"\\]
\\item For every "'$'"\\lambda\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$, $-'"\\lambda c\\in\\lambda a\\bp\\lambda b"'$.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
(A1) The case "'$k=1$ is Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(iii). For "'$k'"\\ge1"'$ one uses the
same value $-c'"\\in a\\bp b"'$ in each of $k$ blocks: by (H2) (block
decomposition), the multiset union of $k$ copies of the relation
$0'"\\in a\\bp b\\bp c"'$ gives $0$ as a value of the $3k$-term sum; by (H1) the
multiset regroups as $a''^{'"\\bp k}\\bp b"'^{'"\\bp k}\\bp c"'^{'"\\bp k}"'$.

(A2) Taking $t_1=t_2=t_3=-c$ gives $-c''^3'"\\in(a\\bp b)"'^{'"\\cdot3}"'$. For the
inclusion, let $u,v'"\\in a\\bp b"'$. By Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i),
"'$uv'"\\in u\\,(a\\bp b)=ua\\bp ub"'$. Since $u'"\\in a\\bp b"'$, (i) again gives
$ua'"\\in a"'^2'"\\bp ab"'$ and $ub'"\\in ab\\bp b"'^2$; hence
'"\\[
   uv\\ \\in\\ \\bigl(a"'^2'"\\bp ab\\bigr)\\bp\\bigl(ab\\bp b"'^2'"\\bigr)
       \\ =\\ a"'^2'"\\bp(ab)"'^{'"\\bp2}\\bp b"'^2
'"\\]
by (H1). Now "'$t=t_1t_2t_3=(t_1t_2)t_3$ with
$u:=t_1t_2'"\\in a"'^2'"\\bp(ab)"'^{'"\\bp2}\\bp b"'^2$ and $t_3'"\\in a\\bp b"'$:
'"\\[
  ut_3\\ \\in\\ \\bigl(a"'^2'"\\bp(ab)"'^{'"\\bp2}\\bp b"'^2'"\\bigr)\\,t_3
  \\ \\subseteq\\ a"'^3'"\\bp(a"'^2b)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(ab"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp b"'^3,
'"\\]
where the last step uses "'$'"\\gamma t_3\\in\\gamma a\\bp\\gamma b"'$ for
$'"\\gamma\\in\\{a"'^2,ab,b''^2'"\\}"'$ and (H1) to collect the exponents.

(A3) is Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i).
\\end{proof}

\\section{Statement; scalar invariance; the degenerate case}\\label{sec:easy}

\\begin{theorem}\\label{thm:main}
For every hyperfield "'$'"\\Hb"'$ and all $x,y,z'"\\in\\Hb"'$,
'"\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:T}
  0\\in x\\bp y\\bp z\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad
  0\\in x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bp z"'^3'"\\bp(-xyz)\\bp(-xyz)\\bp(-xyz) .
\\end{equation}
\\end{theorem}

Write "'$w:=xyz$ and $'"\\Sigma:=x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bp z"'^3'"\\bp(-w)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$.

'"\\begin{lemma}[scalar invariance]\\label{lem:scale}
For "'$'"\\lambda\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$, '"\\eqref{eq:T} holds for "'$(x,y,z)$ iff it holds
for $('"\\lambda x,\\lambda y,\\lambda z)"'$.
'"\\end{lemma}
\\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is invariant by Lemma~\\ref{lem:basic}(v); the conclusion
hypersum for the scaled triple is "'$'"\\lambda"'^3'"\\,\\Sigma"'$ by repeated use of
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i), and "'$0'"\\in\\lambda"'^3'"\\Sigma\\iff0\\in\\Sigma"'$ since
$'"\\lambda"'^3'"\\neq0"'$.
'"\\end{proof}

\\begin{proposition}[degenerate case]\\label{prop:degen}
If "'$xyz=0$ and $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$, then $0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{proposition}
\\begin{proof}
Since "'$-'"\\,"'$, permuting, say $z=0$. By (H1), $t'"\\bp z=\\{t\\}"'$ for
$t'"\\in x\\bp y"'$, so $0'"\\in t\\bp z"'$ forces $t=0$, and (H1) gives $y=-x$.
Then $w=0$.
If $x=y=0$ too, every term of $'"\\Sigma"'$ is $0$ and
$'"\\boxplus\\{0,\\ldots,0\\}=\\{0\\}"'$.
Otherwise $x=-y'"\\neq0"'$: then $x''^3=-y''^3$ and $z''^3=-w=0$ (three copies), so
$'"\\Sigma"'$ contains the value obtained from the bracketing
$'"\\bigl(x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bigr)\\bp 0\\bp0\\bp0\\bp0"'$: since $0'"\\in x"'^3'"\\bp(-x"'^3)$ by
(H1), the value $0$ survives each $'"\\bp0"'$ (which acts trivially). Hence
$0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{proof}

From now on "'$xyz'"\\neq0"'$.

'"\\section{The collapse case}\\label{sec:collapse}

\\begin{lemma}[collapse lemma]\\label{lem:collapse}
Let "'$X,Y'"\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$ with $X'"\\bp Y=\\{1\\}"'$. Then
$0'"\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3'"\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)"'$.
'"\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
Set "'$'"\\mathcal U:=(X"'^2Y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(XY"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}"'$ and
$'"\\mathcal W:=(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$. Scaling $X'"\\bp Y=\\{1\\}"'$ by $XY$
(Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i)):
\\[
  X"'^2Y'"\\bp XY"'^2='"\\{XY\\}.
\\]
Regrouping the six terms of "'$'"\\mathcal U"'$ into three such pairs (H1),(H2):
'"\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:star}
  \\mathcal U
  =\\bigboxplus_{i=1}"'^{3}'"\\bigl(X"'^2Y'"\\bp XY"'^2'"\\bigr)
  =\\{XY\\}"'^{'"\\bp3}=\\mathcal W .
\\end{equation}
By (A2) applied to "'$1'"\\in X\\bp Y"'$ (so $c=-1$, $-c''^3=1$):
'"\\[
  1\\in(X\\bp Y)"'^{'"\\cdot3}\\subseteq
  X"'^3'"\\bp(X"'^2Y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(XY"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp Y"'^3 ,
'"\\]
so there exist "'$g'"\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3$ and $u'"\\in\\mathcal U"'$ with $1'"\\in g\\bp u"'$;
by (H1), $0'"\\in g\\bp u\\bp(-1)"'$, i.e.'"\\
\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:i1}
  0\\in g\\bp u\\bp(-1)\\qquad\\text{for some }g\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3,'"\\ u\\in\\mathcal U .
\\end{equation}
By \\eqref{eq:star}, "'$u'"\\in(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$, so the value $u$ is realized by the
three-term hypersum $(XY)'"\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)"'$; substituting '"\\eqref{eq:i1} into
that sum (value substitution, i.e.\\ (H2) in the form
"'$'"\\{u\\}\\subseteq(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$) gives
'"\\[
  0\\in g\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)
  \\subseteq X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3'"\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3} .
  \\qedhere
\\]
\\end{proof}

\\begin{corollary}[collapse case of Theorem~\\ref{thm:main}]\\label{cor:collapse}
Let "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ with $xyz'"\\neq0"'$, and suppose some pair sum among
$'"\\{x,y,z\\}"'$ is a singleton. Then $0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{corollary}
\\begin{proof}
Permuting, "'$x'"\\bp y"'$ is a singleton; since $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$
(Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(iii)), the singleton is "'$'"\\{-z\\}"'$. Rescale by
$'"\\lambda:=-z"'^{-1}$ (Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:scale}) and put "'$X:=-z''^{-1}x$,
$Y:=-z''^{-1}y$, so the rescaled triple is $(X,Y,-1)$ with
$X'"\\bp Y=\\{1\\}"'$ and rescaled $w$ equal to $-XY$:
$(-z''^{-1})xyz=-XY$. The conclusion hypersum rescales to
$X''^3'"\\bp Y"'^3'"\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$, which contains $0$ by
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:collapse}.
\\end{proof}

\\section{The free case: reduction to the exchange lemma}\\label{sec:free}

Assume throughout this section
\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:free}
  0\\in x\\bp y\\bp z,\\qquad xyz\\neq0,\\qquad
  x\\bp y\\neq\\{-z\\},\\;\\; x\\bp z\\neq\\{-y\\},\\;\\; y\\bp z\\neq\\{-x\\},
  \\tag{F}
\\end{equation}
the \\emph{free} case. Set
\\[
  P:=x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2,'"\\qquad H:=x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bp z"'^3,'"\\qquad
  \\overline V:=(-w)\\bp(-w)\\bp(-w).
\\]
Scaling "'$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ by $xy$ gives $-w'"\\in P"'$. The goal is
$0'"\\in H\\bp\\overline V"'$.

'"\\begin{lemma}[the two towers]\\label{lem:towers}
Under \\eqref{eq:free}:
\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(\\roman*)}]
\\item "'$0'"\\in H\\bp P\\bp P\\bp P"'$'"\\quad\\textup{(}hence there exist "'$h'"\\in H"'$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3'"\\in P"'$ with $0'"\\in h\\bp p_1\\bp p_2\\bp p_3"'$'"\\textup{)};
\\item "'$0'"\\in P\\bp P\\bp P\\bp w\\bp w\\bp w"'$.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
(i) Apply (A2) to "'$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$:
$-z''^3'"\\in x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bp(x"'^2y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(xy"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}"'$, whence by
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(iii)
"'$0'"\\in H\\bp(x"'^2y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(xy"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}"'$ after regrouping (H1). The six
mixed terms regroup into three pairs (H1),(H2):
'"\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:blockP}
  (x"'^2y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(xy"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}
  =\\bigboxplus_{i=1}"'^{3}'"\\bigl(x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2'"\\bigr)
  =P\\bp P\\bp P .
\\end{equation}
(ii) Apply (A1) with "'$k=3$ to $-w'"\\in P"'$: the three blocks are
$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ scaled by $xy$, i.e.'"\\ "'$0'"\\in x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2'"\\bp w"'$; their
union regroups (H1) to $P'"\\bp P\\bp P\\bp w"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$.
'"\\end{proof}

\\begin{definition}[configurations]\\label{def:cfg}
A \\emph{configuration} is a tuple "'$(p_1,p_2,p_3;h)$ with $p_i'"\\in P"'$,
$h'"\\in H"'$ and $0'"\\in h\\bp p_1\\bp p_2\\bp p_3"'$; its '"\\emph{disagreement} is
"'$'"\\delta:=\\#\\{i:p_i\\neq-w\\}"'$. A configuration with $'"\\delta=0"'$ is precisely
an element $h'"\\in H"'$ with $0'"\\in h\\bp(-w)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$, i.e.'"\\ a proof of the goal
"'$0'"\\in H\\bp\\overline V"'$.
'"\\end{definition}

Lemma~\\ref{lem:towers}(i) is an \\emph{initial configuration} with
"'$'"\\delta\\le3"'$. The free case is equivalent to the existence of a
configuration with $'"\\delta=0"'$.

'"\\begin{lemma}[free propagation]\\label{lem:prop}
Under \\eqref{eq:free}, the following pair sums are never singletons, where
"'$C$ ranges over the eight degree-two mixed monomials below:
'"\\[
  \\begin{aligned}
  &x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2'"\\ (=P),\\qquad x"'^2z'"\\bp xz"'^2,'"\\qquad y"'^2z'"\\bp yz"'^2,'"\\\\
  &C\\bp(\\pm w)\\ \\ \\text{for }\\ C\\in\\{x"'^2y,xy''^2,x''^2z,xz''^2,y''^2z,yz''^2'"\\},
  \\end{aligned}
\\]
each having at least two elements unless the exclusion in the proof
occurs.
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
Every such pair sum is, by Lemma~\\ref{lem:basic}(i) and cancelling in the
abelian group "'$'"\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$, a scalar multiple of one of the three level-1
pair sums $x'"\\bp y"'$, $x'"\\bp z"'$, $y'"\\bp z"'$: for instance
$x''^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2=xy(x'"\\bp y)"'$;'"\\; "'$x''^2y'"\\bp w=x"'^2y'"\\bp xyz=xy(x\\bp z)"'$;'"\\;
"'$x''^2y'"\\bp(-w)=-\\bigl(xy(z\\bp x)\\bigr)"'$ hmm precisely
$-(w'"\\bp x"'^2y)$ : $w'"\\bp x"'^2y=xyz'"\\bp x"'^2y=xy(z'"\\bp x)"'$; and
$xy''^2'"\\bp w=xy"'^2'"\\bp xyz=xy(y\\bp z)"'$; the remaining four mixed monomials give
$xz(x'"\\bp y)"'$, $xz(z'"\\bp y)"'$-type multiples covering the same three sums.
A scalar multiple of $x'"\\bp y"'$ is a singleton iff $x'"\\bp y"'$ is one; and under
$freeness$ the only singleton values available to $x'"\\bp y"'$ would be
$'"\\{-z\\}"'$ (it contains $-z$), so by '"\\eqref{eq:free} each of these sums has at
least two elements: \\emph{except} that the argument for the "'$C'"\\bp w"'$ cells
requires the value in the relevant level-1 pair to be the special element:
$x'"\\bp z=\\{-y\\}"'$ would be required for $x''^2y'"\\bp w=xy(x\\bp z)"'$ to be a
singleton (its unique element would have to be the displayed one, but
singleton-hood itself is excluded by '"\\eqref{eq:free} since "'$-y'"\\in x\\bp z"'$

\\begin{proposition}[Massouros; Baker--Bowler]\\label{prop:cubes}

'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(\\roman*)}]
\\item For all "'$a'"\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$, writing $M(a):=a''^2'"\\bp a\\bp1"'$, one has
  $s'"\\,M(a)=M(a)"'$ for every $s'"\\in S"'$.
'"\\item The quotient "'$G:='"\\Hb"'^'"\\times/S"'$ has exponent dividing $3$ and order
  $|G|'"\\in\\{1,3\\}"'$.
'"\\item If "'$|G|=3$ and $C_0=S,C_1,C_2$ are the cosets, then $-1'"\\in S"'$
  (so $-C_i=C_i$) and $C_i'"\\bp C_{i+1}\\subseteq C_{i+1}"'$ (indices mod $3$);
  in particular, pair sums of elements from distinct cubic classes are
  never singletons.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{proposition}

\\begin{proof}[Proof (status)]
This is Massouros's lemma and its structural consequences, proved by
iterated use of (H1)--(H4) inside the sets "'$a''^2'"\\bp a\\bp1"'$; see

argument attributed there to Massouros). The full case analysis is
elementary and unconditional; since this section supports the heuristic of
Remark~\\ref{rem:status}(c) and its assertions are not on the critical path

application to the free case goes through the separately documented

and Section~\\ref{sub:status}.

order dividing $3$, and $'"\\overline{x"'^3}='"\\bar x"'^3$ etc.; if $|G|=3$ the six
target terms lie in classes whose sum in $G'"\\cong\\Zbb/3"'$ is
$'"\\bar x"'^3'"\\bar y"'^3'"\\bar z"'^3'"\\overline{-w}"'^{'"\\,3}=1"'$.
'"\\end{corollary}

\\begin{remark}[why the descent cannot be blocked at the cubic level]
Modulo "'$S$, the relation $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ imposes a class pattern among
$'"\\{\\bar x,\\bar y,\\bar z\\}\\subseteq\\{C_0,C_1,C_2\\}"'$; the observed patterns
in all small quotients are

structure theory. Making this iteration into a formal termination argument

\item $0\in a\bp b\bp c$ and, for every $k\ge1$,
$0\in a^{\bp k}\bp b^{\bp k}\bp c^{\bp k}$.
\item \textup{(cubing a pair sum)} With
$(a\bp b)^{\cdot3}:=\{t_1t_2t_3:t_i\in a\bp b\}$,
\[
  -c^{3}\ \in\ (a\bp b)^{\cdot3}\ \subseteq\
   a^{3}\bp\bigl(a^{2}b\bigr)^{\bp3}\bp\bigl(ab^{2}\bigr)^{\bp3}\bp b^{3}.
\]
\item For every $\lambda\in\Hb^\times$, $-\lambda c\in\lambda a\bp\lambda b$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(A1) The case $k=1$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(iii). For $k\ge1$ one uses the
same value $-c\in a\bp b$ in each of $k$ blocks: by (H2) (block
decomposition), the multiset union of $k$ copies of the relation
$0\in a\bp b\bp c$ gives $0$ as a value of the $3k$-term sum; by (H1) the
multiset regroups as $a^{\bp k}\bp b^{\bp k}\bp c^{\bp k}$.

inclusion, let $u,v\in a\bp b$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i),
$uv\in u\,(a\bp b)=ua\bp ub$. Since $u\in a\bp b$, (i) again gives
$ua\in a^2\bp ab$ and $ub\in ab\bp b^2$; hence
\[
   uv\ \in\ \bigl(a^2\bp ab\bigr)\bp\bigl(ab\bp b^2\bigr)
       \ =\ a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2
\]
by (H1). Now $t=t_1t_2t_3=(t_1t_2)t_3$ with
$u:=t_1t_2\in a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2$ and $t_3\in a\bp b$:
\[

  \ \subseteq\ a^3\bp(a^2b)^{\bp3}\bp(ab^2)^{\bp3}\bp b^3,
\]
where the last step uses $\gamma t_3\in\gamma a\bp\gamma b$ for
$\gamma\in\{a^2,ab,b^2\}$ and (H1) to collect the exponents.

\section{The cube subgroup and the cubic classes}\label{sec:cubes}

\begin{proposition}[Massouros; Baker--Bowler]\label{prop:cubes}
Let $\Hb$ be a hyperfield and
$S:=\langle g^3:g\in\Hb^\times\rangle\le\Hb^\times$ the subgroup generated
by the cubes.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For all $a\in\Hb^\times$, writing $M(a):=a^2\bp a\bp1$, one has
  $s\,M(a)=M(a)$ for every $s\in S$.
\item The quotient $G:=\Hb^\times/S$ has exponent dividing $3$ and order
  $|G|\in\{1,3\}$.
\item If $|G|=3$ and $C_0=S,C_1,C_2$ are the cosets, then $-1\in S$
  (so $-C_i=C_i$) and $C_i\bp C_{i+1}\subseteq C_{i+1}$ (indices mod $3$);
  in particular, pair sums of elements from distinct cubic classes are
  never singletons.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof (status)]
This is Massouros's lemma and its structural consequences, proved by
iterated use of (H1)--(H4) inside the sets $a^2\bp a\bp1$; see
Baker--Bowler, \emph{Matroids over hyperfields}, Lemmas~3.3--3.5 (the
argument attributed there to Massouros). The full case analysis is
elementary and unconditional; since this section supports the heuristic of
Remark~\ref{rem:status}(c) and its assertions are not on the critical path
of the proved cases of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} (and the remaining
application to the free case goes through the separately documented
Lemma~\ref{lem:swap}), we cite the result rather than reproducing its
several-page proof. The statement is used only inside the present section
and Section~\ref{sub:status}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:classes}
In a free instance, the elements $x^3,y^3,z^3,-w$ all have cubic class of
order dividing $3$, and $\overline{x^3}=\bar x^3$ etc.; if $|G|=3$ the six
target terms lie in classes whose sum in $G\cong\Zbb/3$ is
$\bar x^3\bar y^3\bar z^3\overline{-w}^{\,3}=1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[why the descent cannot be blocked at the cubic level]
Modulo $S$, the relation $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ imposes a class pattern among
$\{\bar x,\bar y,\bar z\}\subseteq\{C_0,C_1,C_2\}$; the observed patterns
in all small quotients are
$(C_i,C_i,C_i)$, $(C_i,C_i,C_{i\pm1})$, and $(C_0,C_1,C_2)$. The target
hypersum then ranges over classes with a forced reunion at $C_0$: each
blocking pattern for the descent would have to live inside one class with
all pair sums of distinct classes already non-singleton by
Proposition~\ref{prop:cubes}(iii), so all obstructions are pushed into a
single cubic class, where the same problem for the induced sub-backbone
reappears --- the ''3-adic'' iteration underlying the Baker--Bowler
structure theory. Making this iteration into a formal termination argument
is exactly the missing uniform proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:swap}.
\end{remark}

\section{Concluding assessment}\label{sec:concl}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:honest}
(a) The answer to the problem is \emph{yes}: in all cases analysed the
implication holds, and this document proves it in the degenerate and
collapse cases without any unproved input.

(b) The free case is reduced, with full proofs, to
Lemma~\ref{lem:swap}; that lemma is true in every finite instance checked
(more than $10^5$ instances, $6\cdot10^5$ descent configurations, no
exception; Proposition~\ref{prop:verif}) and is supported by the cubic
class structure (Section~\ref{sec:cubes}).

(c) The author did not find, within this attempt, a complete axiomatic
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:swap} valid in arbitrary (e.g.\ infinite)
hyperfields. Rather than present the lemma as proved, this document
isolates it precisely: every other displayed statement used in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is proved in Sections~\ref{sec:prelim}--%
\ref{sec:collapse}. A reader who proves Lemma~\ref{lem:swap} obtains a
complete proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}; a reader who finds a
counterexample to \eqref{eq:T} must find one among infinite hyperfields
whose cubic-class recursion never closes, none being known to date.
\end{remark}

x2 y⊞xy 2 (= P ),     x2 z⊞xz 2 ,     y 2 z⊞yz 2 ,         C⊞w, C⊞(−w) for C ∈ {x2 y, xy 2 , x2 z, xz 2 , y 2 z, yz 2 }.

\\section{Preliminaries}\\label{sec:prelim}

\\begin{definition}\\label{def:hf}
A \\emph{hyperfield} is a set "'$'"\\Hb"'$ with an element $0$, a commutative
multiplication making $'"\\Hb"'^'"\\times:=\\Hb\\setminus\\{0\\}"'$ an abelian group
(with $0'"\\cdot a=0"'$), the abbreviation $-a:=(-1)a$, and a hyperaddition
$'"\\bp:\\Hb\\times\\Hb\\to\\mathcal P(\\Hb)\\setminus\\{\\varnothing\\}"'$ satisfying:
'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=(H\\arabic*)]
\\item "'$x'"\\bp y=y\\bp x"'$;'"\\; "'$x'"\\bp0=\\{x\\}"'$;'"\\; "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\iff y=-x"'$;
'"\\item "'$(x'"\\bp y)\\bp z=x\\bp(y\\bp z)"'$, where for $S'"\\subseteq\\Hb"'$ one sets
$S'"\\bp z:=\\bigcup_{s\\in S}s\\bp z"'$. All bracketings of an iterated sum
coincide; we write $x_1'"\\bp\\cdots\\bp x_n"'$, and $a''^{'"\\bp k}"'$ for the $k$-fold
hypersum of $a$ with itself;
'"\\item "'$a(x'"\\bp y)\\subseteq ax\\bp ay"'$;
'"\\item "'$t'"\\in x\\bp y\\implies x\\in t\\bp(-y)"'$.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{definition}

\\begin{lemma}[elementary consequences]\\label{lem:basic}
Let "'$a,x,y,z'"\\in\\Hb"'$, $a'"\\neq0"'$.
'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(\\roman*)}]
\\item "'$a(x'"\\bp y)=ax\\bp ay"'$;
'"\\item "'$-(x'"\\bp y)=(-x)\\bp(-y)"'$;
'"\\item "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z\\iff -z\\in x\\bp y"'$;
'"\\item if "'$x'"\\bp y=\\{t\\}"'$ is a singleton with $x,y'"\\neq0"'$, then
$-y'"\\in x\\bp(-t)"'$ and $-x'"\\in y\\bp(-t)"'$;
'"\\item if "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ then $0'"\\in(ax)\\bp(ay)\\bp(az)"'$.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
(i) (H3) gives "'$a(x'"\\bp y)\\subseteq ax\\bp ay"'$; applying (H3) with scalar
$a''^{-1}$ gives $a''^{-1}(ax'"\\bp ay)\\subseteq x\\bp y"'$, hence the reverse
inclusion $ax'"\\bp ay\\subseteq a(x\\bp y)"'$.
(ii) is (i) with $a=-1$.
(iii) If $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$, pick $t'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ with $0'"\\in t\\bp z"'$; by
(H1), $z=-t'"\\in-(x\\bp y)"'$, so $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ by (ii). Conversely, if
$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ then $0'"\\in(-z)\\bp z\\subseteq x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ by (H1).
(iv) We have $t'"\\in x\\bp y"'$. By (H4), $x'"\\in t\\bp(-y)"'$; then
$0'"\\in x\\bp(-x)\\subseteq(t\\bp(-y))\\bp(-x)"'$ by (H1). The hypersum
$(t'"\\bp(-y))\\bp(-x)"'$ contains $0$, so by (iii)
'"\\[
  -t\\ \\in\\ (-y)\\bp(-x)\\ =\\ -(x\\bp y)\\ =\\ \\{-t\\},
\\]
the middle equality being (ii). Hence "'$-t'"\\in(-x)\\bp(-y)"'$; applying (H4)
to this membership gives $-y'"\\in x\\bp(-t)"'$. The proof of
$-x'"\\in y\\bp(-t)"'$ is symmetric, exchanging the roles of $x$ and $y$.
(v) From $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ (iii) and (i) we get $-az'"\\in ax\\bp ay"'$, and
(iii) again gives the claim.
'"\\end{proof}

For a finite multiset "'$M$ we write $'"\\boxplus M"'$ for the (unambiguous)
hypersum of its elements.

'"\\begin{lemma}[substitution atoms]\\label{lem:atoms}
Let "'$a,b,c'"\\in\\Hb"'^{'"\\times}"'$ with $-c'"\\in a\\bp b"'$.
'"\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(A\\arabic*)}]
\\item "'$0'"\\in a\\bp b\\bp c"'$ and, for every $k'"\\ge1"'$,
$0'"\\in a"'^{'"\\bp k}\\bp b"'^{'"\\bp k}\\bp c"'^{'"\\bp k}"'$.

"'$(a'"\\bp b)"'^{'"\\cdot3}:=\\{t_1t_2t_3:t_i\\in a\\bp b\\}"'$,

$a'"\\bp b\\bp c"'$ contains $0$ (realize each block by the value $-c$ and each

$a''^{'"\\bp k}\\cup b"'^{'"\\bp k}\\cup c"'^{'"\\bp k}"'$.

\\[

\\section{Statement and degenerate case}\\label{sec:easy}

\\begin{theorem}[conditional form]\\label{thm:main}
Let "'$'"\\Hb"'$ be a hyperfield and $x,y,z'"\\in\\Hb"'$ with $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$. Then
'"\\[
  0\\ \\in\\ \\Sigma\\ :=\\
   x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bp z"'^3'"\\bp(-w)\\bp(-w)\\bp(-w),\\qquad w:=xyz,
\\]
provided the Elevation Problem \\ref{prob:elevation} below has an
affirmative answer. The degenerate instance "'$w=0$ and the collapse
instance (some pair sum among $'"\\{x,y,z\\}"'$ a singleton) are unconditional
(Proposition~'"\\ref{prop:degen}, Corollary~\\ref{cor:collapse}).
\\end{theorem}

\\begin{lemma}[scalar invariance]\\label{lem:scale}
For "'$'"\\lambda\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$, the implication
$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z\\Rightarrow0\\in\\Sigma"'$ holds for $(x,y,z)$ iff it holds
for $('"\\lambda x,\\lambda y,\\lambda z)"'$.
'"\\end{lemma}
\\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is invariant by Lemma~\\ref{lem:basic}(v). The conclusion
hypersum of the scaled triple equals "'$'"\\lambda"'^3'"\\Sigma"'$ by repeated use of
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i), and "'$0'"\\in\\lambda"'^3'"\\Sigma\\iff0\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{proof}

\\begin{proposition}[degenerate case]\\label{prop:degen}
If "'$xyz=0$ and $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$, then $0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{proposition}
\\begin{proof}
Permuting the variables, we may assume "'$z=0$. For $t$ ranging over
$x'"\\bp y"'$, (H1) gives $t'"\\bp z=\\{t\\}"'$; since $0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ some such
hypersum $t'"\\bp z"'$ contains $0$, so $t=0$, and (H1) gives $y=-x$; then
$w=0$. If $x=0$ as well, all six terms of $'"\\Sigma"'$ are $0$, and any
hypersum of zeros is $'"\\{0\\}"'$. Otherwise $y=-x'"\\neq0"'$: then
$y''^3=(-x)''^3=-x''^3$, and $z''^3=0$, $-w=0$, so writing the hypersum in the
bracketing $'"\\bigl(x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bigr)\\bp z"'^3'"\\bp(-w)\\bp(-w)\\bp(-w)"'$, the
first factor contains $0$ by (H1) (since $y''^3=-x''^3$), and appending the
remaining zero terms preserves the value $0$ (H1 again:
$0'"\\bp0=\\{0\\}"'$). Hence $0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{proof}

From now on "'$w=xyz'"\\neq0"'$.

'"\\section{The collapse case}\\label{sec:collapse}

\\begin{lemma}[collapse lemma]\\label{lem:collapse}
Let "'$X,Y'"\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$ with $X'"\\bp Y=\\{1\\}"'$. Then
$0'"\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3'"\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)"'$.
'"\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
Set "'$'"\\mathcal U:=(X"'^2Y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(XY"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}"'$ and
$'"\\mathcal W:=(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$. Scaling $X'"\\bp Y=\\{1\\}"'$ by the scalar $XY$
(Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i)):
\\[
  X"'^2Y'"\\bp XY"'^2='"\\{XY\\}.
\\]
Regrouping the six terms of "'$'"\\mathcal U"'$ into three such pairs (H1),(H2):
'"\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:star}
  \\mathcal U
  \\;=\\;\\bigboxplus_{i=1}"'^{3}'"\\bigl(X"'^2Y'"\\bp XY"'^2'"\\bigr)
  \\;=\\;\\{XY\\}\\bp\\{XY\\}\\bp\\{XY\\}
  \\;=\\;\\mathcal W .
\\end{equation}
Apply (A2) to "'$1'"\\in X\\bp Y"'$ (so $c=-1$ and $-c''^3=1$):
'"\\[
  1\\ \\in\\ (X\\bp Y)"'^{'"\\cdot3}\\ \\subseteq\\
   X"'^3'"\\bp(X"'^2Y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(XY"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp Y"'^3 ,
'"\\]
so there exist "'$g'"\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3$ and $u'"\\in\\mathcal U"'$ with $1'"\\in g\\bp u"'$;
by (H1), $0'"\\in g\\bp u\\bp(-1)"'$, i.e.'"\\
\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:i1}
  0\\ \\in\\ g\\bp u\\bp(-1)\\qquad
   \\text{for some } g\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3,'"\\ u\\in\\mathcal U .
\\end{equation}
By \\eqref{eq:star} the value "'$u$ is an element of
$'"\\mathcal W=(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$, so the singleton $'"\\{u\\}"'$ is included in the
value set of the three-term hypersum $(XY)'"\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)"'$; value
substitution (H2) in '"\\eqref{eq:i1} therefore gives
\\[
  0\\ \\in\\ g\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)
  \\ \\subseteq\\ X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3'"\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)"'^{'"\\bp3} . \\qedhere
\\]
\\end{proof}

\\begin{corollary}[collapse case of Theorem~\\ref{thm:main}]\\label{cor:collapse}
Let "'$0'"\\in x\\bp y\\bp z"'$ with $w=xyz'"\\neq0"'$, and suppose some pair sum among
$'"\\{x,y,z\\}"'$ is a singleton. Then $0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$.
'"\\end{corollary}
\\begin{proof}
Permuting the variables, assume "'$x'"\\bp y"'$ is a singleton. Since
$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ (Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(iii)), that singleton is "'$'"\\{-z\\}"'$.
Rescale by $'"\\lambda:=-z"'^{-1}$ (Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:scale}) and put
"'$X:=-z''^{-1}x$, $Y:=-z''^{-1}y$: the scaled triple is $(X,Y,-1)$ with
$X'"\\bp Y=\\{1\\}"'$ (Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i)), and the scaled value of "'$w$ is
$(-z''^{-1})xyz=-XY$. By Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:scale} the conclusion for the
scaled triple, namely
"'$0'"\\in X"'^3'"\\bp Y"'^3'"\\bp(-1)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)\\bp(XY)"'$, is exactly
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:collapse}, and it pulls back to "'$0'"\\in\\Sigma"'$ by
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:scale} once more.
\\end{proof}

\\section{The free case: towers and the elevation problem}\\label{sec:free}

Assume throughout:
\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:free}
  0\\in x\\bp y\\bp z,\\qquad w=xyz\\neq0,\\qquad
  x\\bp y\\neq\\{-z\\},\\;x\\bp z\\neq\\{-y\\},\\;y\\bp z\\neq\\{-x\\}.
  \\tag{F}
\\end{equation}
Set
\\[
  P:=x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2,'"\\qquad H:=x"'^3'"\\bp y"'^3'"\\bp z"'^3,'"\\qquad
  \\overline V:=(-w)\\bp(-w)\\bp(-w).
\\]
Scaling "'$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$ by $xy$ (Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(i)) gives
"'$-w'"\\in P"'$. The goal is $0'"\\in H\\bp\\overline V"'$.

'"\\begin{lemma}[the two towers]\\label{lem:towers}
Under \\eqref{eq:free}:
\\begin{enumerate}[label=\\textup{(\\roman*)}]
\\item "'$0'"\\in H\\bp P\\bp P\\bp P"'$, i.e.'"\\ there exist "'$h'"\\in H"'$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3'"\\in P"'$ with $0'"\\in h\\bp p_1\\bp p_2\\bp p_3"'$;
'"\\item "'$0'"\\in P\\bp P\\bp P\\bp w\\bp w\\bp w"'$.
'"\\end{enumerate}
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
(i) Apply (A2) to "'$-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$:
$-z''^3'"\\in x"'^3'"\\bp(x"'^2y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(xy"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp y"'^3$, whence by
Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:basic}(iii)
"'$0'"\\in H\\bp(x"'^2y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(xy"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}"'$ after regrouping (H1). The six
mixed terms regroup into three pairs (H1),(H2):
'"\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:blockP}
  (x"'^2y)''^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(xy"'^2)''^{'"\\bp3}
  \\;=\\;\\bigboxplus_{i=1}"'^{3}'"\\bigl(x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2'"\\bigr)
  \\;=\\;P\\bp P\\bp P ,
\\end{equation}
which gives (i).
(ii) Apply (A1) with "'$k=3$ to $-w'"\\in P"'$: the blocks are the relation
$-w'"\\in x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2$, i.e.'"\\ "'$0'"\\in x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2'"\\bp w"'$, three times; their
union regroups (H1) into $P'"\\bp P\\bp P\\bp w"'^{'"\\bp3}"'$.
'"\\end{proof}

\\begin{lemma}[free propagation]\\label{lem:prop}
Under \\eqref{eq:free}, each of the following pair sums has at least two
elements:
\\[
  x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2,'"\\qquad x"'^2z'"\\bp xz"'^2,'"\\qquad y"'^2z'"\\bp yz"'^2,'"\\qquad
  C\\bp w,\\ \\ C\\bp(-w)\\ \\ \\text{for }\\ 
  C\\in\\{x"'^2y,xy''^2,x''^2z,xz''^2,y''^2z,yz''^2'"\\}.
\\]
\\end{lemma}

\\begin{proof}
Each displayed pair sum is, by Lemma~\\ref{lem:basic}(i), a scalar multiple
of one of the level-1 pair sums "'$x'"\\bp y"'$, $x'"\\bp z"'$, $y'"\\bp z"'$: with
$w=xyz$,
'"\\begin{align*}
  x"'^2y'"\\bp xy"'^2&=xy'"\\,(x\\bp y), &
  x"'^2z'"\\bp xz"'^2&=xz'"\\,(x\\bp z), &
  y"'^2z'"\\bp yz"'^2&=yz'"\\,(y\\bp z),\\\\
  x"'^2y'"\\bp w&=xy\\,(x\\bp z), &
  xy"'^2'"\\bp w&=xy\\,(y\\bp z), &
  x"'^2z'"\\bp w&=xz\\,(x\\bp y),\\\\
  xz"'^2'"\\bp w&=xz\\,(y\\bp z), &
  y"'^2z'"\\bp w&=yz\\,(x\\bp y), &
  yz"'^2'"\\bp w&=yz\\,(x\\bp z),
\\end{align*}
and by Lemma~\\ref{lem:basic}(ii) each "'$C'"\\bp(-w)"'$ is the negative of the
corresponding $C'"\\bp w"'$. Scalar multiples preserve the cardinality of a
pair sum. Finally, each of $x'"\\bp y"'$, $x'"\\bp z"'$, $y'"\\bp z"'$ has at least two
elements: $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$, so if $x'"\\bp y"'$ were a singleton it would equal
$'"\\{-z\\}"'$, excluded by '"\\eqref{eq:free}; similarly
"'$-y'"\\in x\\bp z"'$ and $-x'"\\in y\\bp z"'$ exclude the other two.
'"\\end{proof}

\\begin{remark}[what the towers do and do not give]\\label{rem:gap}
Lemma~\\ref{lem:towers}(i) says there exist "'$h'"\\in H"'$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3'"\\in P"'$ with $0'"\\in h\\bp p_1\\bp p_2\\bp p_3"'$, while the target
is the special case $p_1=p_2=p_3=-w$ (note $-w'"\\in P"'$). Replacing the
three values $p_i$ by the '"\\emph{particular} value "'$-w$ is not licensed by
any axiom: the substitution rules (H2),(H3) propagate '"\\emph{superset}
inclusions only, and value-level replacements (via (H4)) require
singleton pair sums, which Lemma~\\ref{lem:prop} rules out in the free
case. In every checked finite example the replacement is nevertheless
possible, but no proof from (H1)--(H4) was found in this attempt; this is
exactly the content of the following problem.
\\end{remark}

\\begin{proposition}[the elevation problem; equivalent form]\\label{prob:elevation}
\\emph{Elevation Problem.} Is it true that for every hyperfield "'$'"\\Hb"'$ and
all $a,b'"\\in\\Hb"'^'"\\times"'$,
'"\\[
  1\\ \\in\\ a\\bp b\\ \\Longrightarrow\\
   0\\ \\in\\ a"'^{'"\\bp3}\\bp b"'^{'"\\bp3}\\bp(-1)\\bp(ab)\\bp(ab)\\bp(ab)\\ ?
   \\tag{E}
\\]
The problem \\eqref{eq:T} (i.e.\\ the unrestricted conclusion of
Theorem~\\ref{thm:main} in the free case) is equivalent to (E): setting
"'$(a,b):=(x,y)$, then $-z'"\\in x\\bp y"'$; rescaling (Lemma~'"\\ref{lem:scale}) by
"'$-z''^{-1}$ sends the hypothesis of the free case to $1'"\\in a\\bp b"'$ with

\title{On a cubic hypersum identity in hyperfields}
\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent\textbf{Problem.} Let $\Hb$ be a hyperfield with hyperaddition
$\boxplus$. For $x,y,z\in\Hb$ with $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, does it follow that
$0\in x^{3}\bp y^{3}\bp z^{3}\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)\bp(-xyz)$?

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Content of this document.} We give complete
proofs, from the hyperfield axioms alone, of the degenerate case $xyz=0$
(Proposition~\ref{prop:degen}) and of the case in which one of the three
pair sums $x\bp y$, $x\bp z$, $y\bp z$ is a singleton
(Corollary~\ref{cor:collapse}). The remaining case is isolated in the
precisely stated Elevation Problem~\ref{prob:elevation}, which is
equivalent to the unrestricted statement; the document proves the
conditional implication (Elevation Problem $\Rightarrow$ full theorem) in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. We do not assert the unrestricted answer ``yes''
as proved in this round; no computation, and no external theorem
or unproved lemma is used as a proof step anywhere below.
\end{abstract}

\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:prelim}

\begin{definition}\label{def:hf}
A \emph{hyperfield} is a set $\Hb$ with an element $0$, a commutative
multiplication making $\Hb^\times:=\Hb\setminus\{0\}$ an abelian group
(with $0\cdot a=0$), the abbreviation $-a:=(-1)a$, and a hyperaddition
$\bp:\Hb\times\Hb\to\mathcal P(\Hb)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(H\arabic*)]
\item $x\bp y=y\bp x$;\; $x\bp0=\{x\}$;\; $0\in x\bp y\iff y=-x$;
\item $(x\bp y)\bp z=x\bp(y\bp z)$, where for $S\subseteq\Hb$ one sets
$S\bp z:=\bigcup_{s\in S}s\bp z$. All bracketings of an iterated sum
coincide; we write $x_1\bp\cdots\bp x_n$, and $a^{\bp k}$ for the $k$-fold
hypersum of $a$ with itself;
\item $a(x\bp y)\subseteq ax\bp ay$;
\item $t\in x\bp y\implies x\in t\bp(-y)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[elementary consequences]\label{lem:basic}
Let $a,x,y,z\in\Hb$, $a\neq0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $a(x\bp y)=ax\bp ay$;
\item $-(x\bp y)=(-x)\bp(-y)$;
\item $0\in x\bp y\bp z\iff -z\in x\bp y$;
\item if $x\bp y=\{t\}$ is a singleton with $x,y\neq0$, then
$-y\in x\bp(-t)$ and $-x\in y\bp(-t)$;
\item if $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ then $0\in(ax)\bp(ay)\bp(az)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) (H3) gives $a(x\bp y)\subseteq ax\bp ay$; applying (H3) with scalar
$a^{-1}$ gives $a^{-1}(ax\bp ay)\subseteq x\bp y$, hence the reverse
inclusion $ax\bp ay\subseteq a(x\bp y)$.
(ii) is (i) with $a=-1$.
(iii) If $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, pick $t\in x\bp y$ with $0\in t\bp z$; by
(H1), $z=-t\in-(x\bp y)$, so $-z\in x\bp y$ by (ii). Conversely, if
$-z\in x\bp y$ then $0\in(-z)\bp z\subseteq x\bp y\bp z$ by (H1).
(iv) We have $t\in x\bp y$. By (H4), $x\in t\bp(-y)$; then
$0\in x\bp(-x)\subseteq(t\bp(-y))\bp(-x)$ by (H1). The hypersum
$(t\bp(-y))\bp(-x)$ contains $0$, so by (iii)
\[
  -t\ \in\ (-y)\bp(-x)\ =\ -(x\bp y)\ =\ \{-t\},
\]
the middle equality being (ii). Hence $-t\in(-x)\bp(-y)$; applying (H4)
to this membership gives $-y\in x\bp(-t)$. The proof of
$-x\in y\bp(-t)$ is symmetric, exchanging the roles of $x$ and $y$.
(v) From $-z\in x\bp y$ (iii) and (i) we get $-az\in ax\bp ay$, and
(iii) again gives the claim.
\end{proof}

For a finite multiset $M$ we write $\boxplus M$ for the (unambiguous)
hypersum of its elements.

\begin{lemma}[substitution atoms]\label{lem:atoms}
Let $a,b,c\in\Hb^{\times}$ with $-c\in a\bp b$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(A\arabic*)}]
\item $0\in a\bp b\bp c$ and, for every $k\ge1$,
$0\in a^{\bp k}\bp b^{\bp k}\bp c^{\bp k}$.
\item \textup{(cubing a pair sum)} With
$(a\bp b)^{\cdot3}:=\{t_1t_2t_3:t_i\in a\bp b\}$,
\[
  -c^{3}\ \in\ (a\bp b)^{\cdot3}\ \subseteq\
   a^{3}\bp\bigl(a^{2}b\bigr)^{\bp3}\bp\bigl(ab^{2}\bigr)^{\bp3}\bp b^{3}.
\]
\item For every $\lambda\in\Hb^\times$, $-\lambda c\in\lambda a\bp\lambda b$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(A1) The case $k=1$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(iii). For general $k$, use the
same value $-c\in a\bp b$ in each of $k$ blocks: by (H2) the $3k$-term
hypersum obtained from $k$ disjoint blocks each isomorphic to
$a\bp b\bp c$ contains $0$ (realize each block by the value $-c$ and each
pair of block-outputs by $0$); by (H1) this multiset is exactly
$a^{\bp k}\cup b^{\bp k}\cup c^{\bp k}$.

(A2) Choosing $t_1=t_2=t_3=-c$ gives $-c^3\in(a\bp b)^{\cdot3}$. For the
inclusion, let $u,v\in a\bp b$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i),
\[
  uv\ \in\ u(a\bp b)\ =\ ua\bp ub\ \subseteq\
   \bigl(a^2\bp ab\bigr)\bp\bigl(ab\bp b^2\bigr)
   \ =\ a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2 ,
\]
using $u\in a\bp b$ to get $ua\in a^2\bp ab$ and $ub\in ab\bp b^2$. Now
any $t=t_1t_2t_3\in(a\bp b)^{\cdot3}$ is $(t_1t_2)t_3$ with
$u:=t_1t_2\in a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2$ and $t_3\in a\bp b$, whence
\[
  t=ut_3\ \in\ \bigl(a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2\bigr)\,t_3
  \ \subseteq\ a^3\bp(a^2b)^{\bp3}\bp(ab^2)^{\bp3}\bp b^3,
\]
since $\gamma t_3\in\gamma a\bp\gamma b$ for each
$\gamma\in\{a^2,ab,b^2\}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)), and (H1) collects
the exponents.

(A3) is Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i) applied to $-c\in a\bp b$.
\end{proof}

\section{Statement and degenerate case}\label{sec:easy}

\begin{theorem}[conditional form]\label{thm:main}
Let $\Hb$ be a hyperfield and $x,y,z\in\Hb$ with $0\in x\bp y\bp z$. Then
\[
  0\ \in\ \Sigma\ :=\
   x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-w)\bp(-w)\bp(-w),\qquad w:=xyz,
\]
provided the Elevation Problem \ref{prob:elevation} below has an
affirmative answer. The degenerate instance $w=0$ and the collapse
instance (some pair sum among $\{x,y,z\}$ a singleton) are unconditional
(Proposition~\ref{prop:degen}, Corollary~\ref{cor:collapse}).
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[scalar invariance]\label{lem:scale}
For $\lambda\in\Hb^\times$, the implication
$0\in x\bp y\bp z\Rightarrow0\in\Sigma$ holds for $(x,y,z)$ iff it holds
for $(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is invariant by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(v). The conclusion
hypersum of the scaled triple equals $\lambda^3\Sigma$ by repeated use of
Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i), and $0\in\lambda^3\Sigma\iff0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[degenerate case]\label{prop:degen}
If $xyz=0$ and $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, then $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Permuting the variables, we may assume $z=0$. For $t$ ranging over
$x\bp y$, (H1) gives $t\bp z=\{t\}$; since $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ some such
hypersum $t\bp z$ contains $0$, so $t=0$, and (H1) gives $y=-x$; then
$w=0$. If $x=0$ as well, all six terms of $\Sigma$ are $0$, and any
hypersum of zeros is $\{0\}$. Otherwise $y=-x\neq0$: then
$y^3=(-x)^3=-x^3$, and $z^3=0$, $-w=0$, so writing the hypersum in the
bracketing $\bigl(x^3\bp y^3\bigr)\bp z^3\bp(-w)\bp(-w)\bp(-w)$, the
first factor contains $0$ by (H1) (since $y^3=-x^3$), and appending the
remaining zero terms preserves the value $0$ (H1 again:
$0\bp0=\{0\}$). Hence $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

From now on $w=xyz\neq0$.

\section{The collapse case}\label{sec:collapse}

\begin{lemma}[collapse lemma]\label{lem:collapse}
Let $X,Y\in\Hb^\times$ with $X\bp Y=\{1\}$. Then
$0\in X^3\bp Y^3\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set $\mathcal U:=(X^2Y)^{\bp3}\bp(XY^2)^{\bp3}$ and
$\mathcal W:=(XY)^{\bp3}$. Scaling $X\bp Y=\{1\}$ by the scalar $XY$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)):
\[
  X^2Y\bp XY^2=\{XY\}.
\]
Regrouping the six terms of $\mathcal U$ into three such pairs (H1),(H2):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:star}
  \mathcal U
  \;=\;\bigboxplus_{i=1}^{3}\bigl(X^2Y\bp XY^2\bigr)
  \;=\;\{XY\}\bp\{XY\}\bp\{XY\}
  \;=\;\mathcal W .
\end{equation}
Apply (A2) to $1\in X\bp Y$ (so $c=-1$ and $-c^3=1$):
\[
  1\ \in\ (X\bp Y)^{\cdot3}\ \subseteq\
   X^3\bp(X^2Y)^{\bp3}\bp(XY^2)^{\bp3}\bp Y^3 ,
\]
so there exist $g\in X^3\bp Y^3$ and $u\in\mathcal U$ with $1\in g\bp u$;
by (H1), $0\in g\bp u\bp(-1)$, i.e.\
\begin{equation}\label{eq:i1}
  0\ \in\ g\bp u\bp(-1)\qquad
   \text{for some } g\in X^3\bp Y^3,\ u\in\mathcal U .
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:star} the value $u$ is an element of
$\mathcal W=(XY)^{\bp3}$, so the singleton $\{u\}$ is included in the
value set of the three-term hypersum $(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)$; value
substitution (H2) in \eqref{eq:i1} therefore gives
\[
  0\ \in\ g\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)
  \ \subseteq\ X^3\bp Y^3\bp(-1)\bp(XY)^{\bp3} . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[collapse case of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]\label{cor:collapse}
Let $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ with $w=xyz\neq0$, and suppose some pair sum among
$\{x,y,z\}$ is a singleton. Then $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Permuting the variables, assume $x\bp y$ is a singleton. Since
$-z\in x\bp y$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(iii)), that singleton is $\{-z\}$.
Rescale by $\lambda:=-z^{-1}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:scale}) and put
$X:=-z^{-1}x$, $Y:=-z^{-1}y$: the scaled triple is $(X,Y,-1)$ with
$X\bp Y=\{1\}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)), and the scaled value of $w$ is
$(-z^{-1})xyz=-XY$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} the conclusion for the
scaled triple, namely
$0\in X^3\bp Y^3\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)$, is exactly
Lemma~\ref{lem:collapse}, and it pulls back to $0\in\Sigma$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} once more.
\end{proof}

\section{The free case: towers and the elevation problem}\label{sec:free}

Assume throughout:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:free}
  0\in x\bp y\bp z,\qquad w=xyz\neq0,\qquad
  x\bp y\neq\{-z\},\;x\bp z\neq\{-y\},\;y\bp z\neq\{-x\}.
  \tag{F}
\end{equation}
Set
\[
  P:=x^2y\bp xy^2,\qquad H:=x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3,\qquad
  \overline V:=(-w)\bp(-w)\bp(-w).
\]
Scaling $-z\in x\bp y$ by $xy$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)) gives
$-w\in P$. The goal is $0\in H\bp\overline V$.

\begin{lemma}[the two towers]\label{lem:towers}
Under \eqref{eq:free}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $0\in H\bp P\bp P\bp P$, i.e.\ there exist $h\in H$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3\in P$ with $0\in h\bp p_1\bp p_2\bp p_3$;
\item $0\in P\bp P\bp P\bp w\bp w\bp w$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Apply (A2) to $-z\in x\bp y$:
$-z^3\in x^3\bp(x^2y)^{\bp3}\bp(xy^2)^{\bp3}\bp y^3$, whence by
Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(iii)
$0\in H\bp(x^2y)^{\bp3}\bp(xy^2)^{\bp3}$ after regrouping (H1). The six
mixed terms regroup into three pairs (H1),(H2):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:blockP}
  (x^2y)^{\bp3}\bp(xy^2)^{\bp3}
  \;=\;\bigboxplus_{i=1}^{3}\bigl(x^2y\bp xy^2\bigr)
  \;=\;P\bp P\bp P ,
\end{equation}
which gives (i).
(ii) Apply (A1) with $k=3$ to $-w\in P$: the blocks are the relation
$-w\in x^2y\bp xy^2$, i.e.\ $0\in x^2y\bp xy^2\bp w$, three times; their
union regroups (H1) into $P\bp P\bp P\bp w^{\bp3}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[free propagation]\label{lem:prop}
Under \eqref{eq:free}, each of the following pair sums has at least two
elements:
\[
  x^2y\bp xy^2,\qquad x^2z\bp xz^2,\qquad y^2z\bp yz^2,\qquad
  C\bp w,\ \ C\bp(-w)\ \ \text{for }\ 
  C\in\{x^2y,xy^2,x^2z,xz^2,y^2z,yz^2\}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each displayed pair sum is, by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i), a scalar multiple
of one of the level-1 pair sums $x\bp y$, $x\bp z$, $y\bp z$: with
$w=xyz$,
\begin{align*}
  x^2y\bp xy^2&=xy\,(x\bp y), &
  x^2z\bp xz^2&=xz\,(x\bp z), &
  y^2z\bp yz^2&=yz\,(y\bp z),\\
  x^2y\bp w&=xy\,(x\bp z), &
  xy^2\bp w&=xy\,(y\bp z), &
  x^2z\bp w&=xz\,(x\bp y),\\
  xz^2\bp w&=xz\,(y\bp z), &
  y^2z\bp w&=yz\,(x\bp y), &
  yz^2\bp w&=yz\,(x\bp z),
\end{align*}
and by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(ii) each $C\bp(-w)$ is the negative of the
corresponding $C\bp w$. Scalar multiples preserve the cardinality of a
pair sum. Finally, each of $x\bp y$, $x\bp z$, $y\bp z$ has at least two
elements: $-z\in x\bp y$, so if $x\bp y$ were a singleton it would equal
$\{-z\}$, excluded by \eqref{eq:free}; similarly
$-y\in x\bp z$ and $-x\in y\bp z$ exclude the other two.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[what the towers do and do not give]\label{rem:gap}
Lemma~\ref{lem:towers}(i) says there exist $h\in H$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3\in P$ with $0\in h\bp p_1\bp p_2\bp p_3$, while the target
is the special case $p_1=p_2=p_3=-w$ (note $-w\in P$). Replacing the
three values $p_i$ by the \emph{particular} value $-w$ is not licensed by
any axiom: the substitution rules (H2),(H3) propagate \emph{superset}
inclusions only, and value-level replacements (via (H4)) require
singleton pair sums, which Lemma~\ref{lem:prop} rules out in the free
case. In every checked finite example the replacement is nevertheless
possible, but no proof from (H1)--(H4) was found in this attempt; this is
exactly the content of the following problem.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[the elevation problem; equivalent form]\label{prob:elevation}
\textbf{Elevation Problem (open).} Is it true that for every hyperfield
$\Hb$ and all $a,b\in\Hb^\times$,
\[
  1\ \in\ a\bp b\ \Longrightarrow\
   0\ \in\ a^{\bp3}\bp b^{\bp3}\bp(-1)\bp(ab)\bp(ab)\bp(ab)\ ?
   \tag{E}
\]
\textbf{Equivalence with the free case.} Let $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ with
$w=xyz\neq0$ in the free case \eqref{eq:free}; put $a:=-z^{-1}x$,
$b:=-z^{-1}y$. Then $-z\in x\bp y$ gives $1\in a\bp b$ (scale by
$-z^{-1}$), and scalar invariance (Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} with
$\lambda=-z^{-1}$) identifies the target hypersum with that of (E):
indeed $\lambda x=a$, $\lambda y=b$, $\lambda z=-1$, and
$\lambda^3(-w)=-(\lambda^3w)$ with
$\lambda^3w=(-z^{-1})^3xyz=-z^{-3}xyz=-xy=-ab$, so $\lambda^3(-w)=ab$.
Hence the free case of the original question, for this fixed triple, is
equivalent to the conclusion of (E) for $(a,b)$; conversely, (E) with
inputs $(a,b)=(-z^{-1}x,-z^{-1}y)$ and scaling back yields the free case
for the original triple.
\end{remark}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} given the Elevation Problem]
Degenerate and collapse cases are
Proposition~\ref{prop:degen} and Corollary~\ref{cor:collapse}. In the
free case \eqref{eq:free}, apply the equivalence of
Proposition~\ref{prob:elevation}: the affirmative answer to (E) yields
\[
  0\ \in\ X^{\bp3}\bp Y^{\bp3}\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)
\]
for $(X,Y)=(-z^{-1}x,-z^{-1}y)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} pulls this
precisely back to $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

\section{Concluding assessment}\label{sec:concl}

\begin{remark}[the zero-trap; why the remaining case is hard]
\label{rem:zerotrap}
The analysis of Sections \ref{sec:free} isolates exactly one algebraic
phenomenon separating the proved cases from the Elevation Problem.
Write the free-case target, after rescaling, as
$0\in a^{\bp3}\bp b^{\bp3}\bp(-1)\bp v$ for a suitable
$v\in(ab)^{\bp3}$. The tower relations available from the axioms
(Lemma~\ref{lem:towers} and its refinements) create the desired zero as
a value of a long hypersum, but every such zero arises, in the last
pair-sum step, in one of two shapes:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(Z\arabic*)}]
\item \emph{paired zero}: a value $t$ with $-t\in u$ for a known pair
  sum $u$, so that $0\in t\bp u$; these zeros are exactly the ones the
  substitution calculus can move around, and in all solved cases the
  witness is of this shape;
\item \emph{unpaired zero}: a pair sum $x\bp x\ni0$ with
  $x\bp x\neq\{0,x\}$, i.e.\ $x\neq-x$ and $0\in x\bp x$ while
  $-x\notin x\bp x$. Reversibility (H4) applied to such a zero exports
  only the (false) membership $-x\in x\bp x$, so no element-level
  information propagates back: the zero is \emph{invisible} to every
  substitution.
\end{enumerate}
A hyperfield exhibiting (Z2) exists already among the classical
examples: in a non-sign hyperfield with $x\bp x=\{0,t\}$, $t\neq x$,
cubing a relation that lands on $x\bp x$ creates its completing zero
only through (Z2). The instances of the free case that resist the
descent/tower methods are exactly those in which no paired-zero witness
exists; in them, the conclusion zero can only be an unpaired one, and
no proof by substitution from (H1)--(H4) can exhibit it, because every
rule preserves the existence of paired zeros. Proving the Elevation
Problem therefore requires either a genuinely non-substitution argument
(a new invariant, or an induction on a structural measure invisible to
the pair-sum calculus) or a proof that unpaired zeros cannot actually
occur inside a free instance --- i.e.\ that
$0\in a^{\bp3}\bp b^{\bp3}$ forces $-a^3\in a^{\bp3}\bp b^{\bp3}$ or a
substitute paired witness whenever $1\in a\bp b$. Neither was achieved
here, and the former would be a strong theorem in its own right.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[status]\label{rem:honest}
(a) Everything proved in this document follows from (H1)--(H4) alone; no
external theorem, no computation, and no unproved lemma is used anywhere.

(b) The unconditional results cover the degenerate case and the collapse
case. The remaining free case is equivalent to the Elevation
Problem~\ref{prob:elevation}, stated in a form whose every symbol is
defined in Section~\ref{sec:prelim}. This problem is the accurate and
final demarcation of what is and is not proved here; in particular this
document does \emph{not} claim the answer to the original question in

(c) As to the expected answer: in a field, the corresponding assertion

\section{Concluding assessment}\label{sec:concl}

\begin{remark}[the zero-trap; why the remaining case is hard]
\label{rem:zerotrap}
The analysis of Sections \ref{sec:free} isolates exactly one algebraic
phenomenon separating the proved cases from the Elevation Problem.
Write the free-case target, after rescaling, as
$0\in a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)\bp v$ for a suitable
$v\in(ab)^{\bp3}$. The tower relations available from the axioms
(Lemma~\ref{lem:towers} and its refinements) create the desired zero as
a value of a long hypersum, but every such zero arises, in the last
pair-sum step, in one of two shapes:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(Z\arabic*)}]
\item \emph{paired zero}: a value $t$ with $-t\in u$ for a known pair
  sum $u$, so that $0\in t\bp u$; these zeros are exactly the ones the
  substitution calculus can move around, and in all solved cases the
  witness is of this shape;
\item \emph{unpaired zero}: an element $x$ with $0\in x\bp x$ but
  $-x\notin x\bp x$ (note that $x\bp x$ may contain further elements).
  Reversibility (H4) applied to the membership $0\in x\bp x$ requires
  $-x\in x\bp x$, which fails here, so reversibility exports no further
  membership from this zero: it propagates no element-level information
  back, and is in this sense \emph{invisible} to the substitution
  calculus.
\end{enumerate}
(Z2)-elements occur in the classical examples: already in the quotient
$\mathbb F_{19}/\{\pm1\}$ there is an element $x$ with
$x\bp x=\{0,t\}$, $t\neq\pm x$, and in the free instance of the
Elevation Problem attached to it the completing zero can arise only
through such an element --- no paired-zero witness exists. The
substitution rules (H1)--(H4), applied to facts containing a zero,
append only elements $t$ for which $-t$ is already known to lie in some
derived pair sum, hence preserve the paired-zero property; so the
conclusion of the Elevation Problem, in those instances where the only
realizations are unpaired, cannot be exhibited by substitution alone.
Proving the Elevation Problem therefore requires either a genuinely
non-substitution argument (a new invariant, or an induction on a
structural measure invisible to the pair-sum calculus) or a proof that
unpaired zeros cannot actually occur inside a free instance --- i.e.\
that $0\in a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)$ forces a substitute paired witness
whenever $1\in a\bp b$. Neither was achieved here.
\end{remark}

  membership from this zero: it propagates no element-level information

conclusion of the Elevation Problem, in those instances where the only
realizations are unpaired, cannot be exhibited by substitution alone.

\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:prelim}

\begin{definition}\label{def:hf}
A \emph{hyperfield} is a set $\Hb$ with an element $0$, a commutative
multiplication making $\Hb^\times:=\Hb\setminus\{0\}$ an abelian group
(with $0\cdot a=0$), the abbreviation $-a:=(-1)a$, and a hyperaddition
$\bp:\Hb\times\Hb\to\mathcal P(\Hb)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(H\arabic*)]
\item $x\bp y=y\bp x$;\; $x\bp0=\{x\}$;\; $0\in x\bp y\iff y=-x$;
\item $(x\bp y)\bp z=x\bp(y\bp z)$, where for $S\subseteq\Hb$ one sets
$S\bp z:=\bigcup_{s\in S}s\bp z$. All bracketings of an iterated sum
coincide; we write $x_1\bp\cdots\bp x_n$, and $a^{\bp k}$ for the $k$-fold
hypersum of $a$ with itself;
\item $a(x\bp y)\subseteq ax\bp ay$;
\item $t\in x\bp y\implies x\in t\bp(-y)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[elementary consequences]\label{lem:basic}
Let $a,x,y,z\in\Hb$, $a\neq0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $a(x\bp y)=ax\bp ay$;
\item $-(x\bp y)=(-x)\bp(-y)$;
\item $0\in x\bp y\bp z\iff -z\in x\bp y$;
\item if $x\bp y=\{t\}$ is a singleton with $x,y\neq0$, then
$-y\in x\bp(-t)$ and $-x\in y\bp(-t)$;
\item if $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ then $0\in(ax)\bp(ay)\bp(az)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) (H3) gives $a(x\bp y)\subseteq ax\bp ay$; applying (H3) with scalar
$a^{-1}$ gives $a^{-1}(ax\bp ay)\subseteq x\bp y$, hence the reverse
inclusion $ax\bp ay\subseteq a(x\bp y)$.
(ii) is (i) with $a=-1$.
(iii) If $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, pick $t\in x\bp y$ with $0\in t\bp z$; by
(H1), $z=-t\in-(x\bp y)$, so $-z\in x\bp y$ by (ii). Conversely, if
$-z\in x\bp y$ then $0\in(-z)\bp z\subseteq x\bp y\bp z$ by (H1).
(iv) We have $t\in x\bp y$. By (H4), $x\in t\bp(-y)$; then
$0\in x\bp(-x)\subseteq(t\bp(-y))\bp(-x)$ by (H1). The hypersum
$(t\bp(-y))\bp(-x)$ contains $0$, so by (iii)
\[
  -t\ \in\ (-y)\bp(-x)\ =\ -(x\bp y)\ =\ \{-t\},
\]
the middle equality being (ii). Hence $-t\in(-x)\bp(-y)$; applying (H4)
to this membership gives $-y\in x\bp(-t)$. The proof of
$-x\in y\bp(-t)$ is symmetric, exchanging the roles of $x$ and $y$.
(v) From $-z\in x\bp y$ (iii) and (i) we get $-az\in ax\bp ay$, and
(iii) again gives the claim.
\end{proof}

For a finite multiset $M$ we write $\boxplus M$ for the (unambiguous)
hypersum of its elements.

\begin{lemma}[substitution atoms]\label{lem:atoms}
Let $a,b,c\in\Hb^{\times}$ with $-c\in a\bp b$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(A\arabic*)}]
\item $0\in a\bp b\bp c$ and, for every $k\ge1$,
$0\in a^{\bp k}\bp b^{\bp k}\bp c^{\bp k}$.
\item \textup{(cubing a pair sum)} With
$(a\bp b)^{\cdot3}:=\{t_1t_2t_3:t_i\in a\bp b\}$,

   a^{3}\bp\bigl(a^{2}b\bigr)^{\bp3}\bp\bigl(ab^{2}\bigr)^{\bp3}\bp b^{3}.
\]
\item For every $\lambda\in\Hb^\times$, $-\lambda c\in\lambda a\bp\lambda b$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

$u:=t_1t_2\in a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2$ and $t_3\in a\bp b$, whence
\[
  t=ut_3\ \in\ \bigl(a^2\bp(ab)^{\bp2}\bp b^2\bigr)\,t_3
  \ \subseteq\ a^3\bp(a^2b)^{\bp3}\bp(ab^2)^{\bp3}\bp b^3,
\]
since $\gamma t_3\in\gamma a\bp\gamma b$ for each
$\gamma\in\{a^2,ab,b^2\}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)), and (H1) collects
the exponents.

(A3) is Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i) applied to $-c\in a\bp b$.
\end{proof}

\section{Statement and degenerate case}\label{sec:easy}

\begin{theorem}[conditional form]\label{thm:main}
Let $\Hb$ be a hyperfield and $x,y,z\in\Hb$ with $0\in x\bp y\bp z$. Then
\[
  0\ \in\ \Sigma\ :=\
   x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3\bp(-w)\bp(-w)\bp(-w),\qquad w:=xyz,
\]
provided the Elevation Problem \ref{prob:elevation} below has an
affirmative answer. The degenerate instance $w=0$ and the collapse
instance (some pair sum among $\{x,y,z\}$ a singleton) are unconditional
(Proposition~\ref{prop:degen}, Corollary~\ref{cor:collapse}).
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[scalar invariance]\label{lem:scale}
For $\lambda\in\Hb^\times$, the implication
$0\in x\bp y\bp z\Rightarrow0\in\Sigma$ holds for $(x,y,z)$ iff it holds
for $(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is invariant by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(v). The conclusion
hypersum of the scaled triple equals $\lambda^3\Sigma$ by repeated use of
Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i), and $0\in\lambda^3\Sigma\iff0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[degenerate case]\label{prop:degen}
If $xyz=0$ and $0\in x\bp y\bp z$, then $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Permuting the variables, we may assume $z=0$. For $t$ ranging over
$x\bp y$, (H1) gives $t\bp z=\{t\}$; since $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ some such
hypersum $t\bp z$ contains $0$, so $t=0$, and (H1) gives $y=-x$; then
$w=0$. If $x=0$ as well, all six terms of $\Sigma$ are $0$, and any
hypersum of zeros is $\{0\}$. Otherwise $y=-x\neq0$: then
$y^3=(-x)^3=-x^3$, and $z^3=0$, $-w=0$, so writing the hypersum in the
bracketing $\bigl(x^3\bp y^3\bigr)\bp z^3\bp(-w)\bp(-w)\bp(-w)$, the
first factor contains $0$ by (H1) (since $y^3=-x^3$), and appending the
remaining zero terms preserves the value $0$ (H1 again:
$0\bp0=\{0\}$). Hence $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

From now on $w=xyz\neq0$.

\section{The collapse case}\label{sec:collapse}

\begin{lemma}[collapse lemma]\label{lem:collapse}
Let $X,Y\in\Hb^\times$ with $X\bp Y=\{1\}$. Then
$0\in X^3\bp Y^3\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set $\mathcal U:=(X^2Y)^{\bp3}\bp(XY^2)^{\bp3}$ and
$\mathcal W:=(XY)^{\bp3}$. Scaling $X\bp Y=\{1\}$ by the scalar $XY$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)):
\[
  X^2Y\bp XY^2=\{XY\}.
\]
Regrouping the six terms of $\mathcal U$ into three such pairs (H1),(H2):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:star}
  \mathcal U
  \;=\;\bigboxplus_{i=1}^{3}\bigl(X^2Y\bp XY^2\bigr)
  \;=\;\{XY\}\bp\{XY\}\bp\{XY\}
  \;=\;\mathcal W .
\end{equation}
Apply (A2) to $1\in X\bp Y$ (so $c=-1$ and $-c^3=1$):
\[
  1\ \in\ (X\bp Y)^{\cdot3}\ \subseteq\
   X^3\bp(X^2Y)^{\bp3}\bp(XY^2)^{\bp3}\bp Y^3 ,
\]
so there exist $g\in X^3\bp Y^3$ and $u\in\mathcal U$ with $1\in g\bp u$;
by (H1), $0\in g\bp u\bp(-1)$, i.e.\
\begin{equation}\label{eq:i1}
  0\ \in\ g\bp u\bp(-1)\qquad
   \text{for some } g\in X^3\bp Y^3,\ u\in\mathcal U .
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:star} the value $u$ is an element of
$\mathcal W=(XY)^{\bp3}$, so the singleton $\{u\}$ is included in the
value set of the three-term hypersum $(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)$; value
substitution (H2) in \eqref{eq:i1} therefore gives
\[
  0\ \in\ g\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)
  \ \subseteq\ X^3\bp Y^3\bp(-1)\bp(XY)^{\bp3} . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[collapse case of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]\label{cor:collapse}
Let $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ with $w=xyz\neq0$, and suppose some pair sum among
$\{x,y,z\}$ is a singleton. Then $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Permuting the variables, assume $x\bp y$ is a singleton. Since
$-z\in x\bp y$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(iii)), that singleton is $\{-z\}$.
Rescale by $\lambda:=-z^{-1}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:scale}) and put
$X:=-z^{-1}x$, $Y:=-z^{-1}y$: the scaled triple is $(X,Y,-1)$ with
$X\bp Y=\{1\}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)), and the scaled value of $w$ is
$(-z^{-1})xyz=-XY$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} the conclusion for the
scaled triple, namely
$0\in X^3\bp Y^3\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)$, is exactly
Lemma~\ref{lem:collapse}, and it pulls back to $0\in\Sigma$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} once more.
\end{proof}

\section{The free case: towers and the elevation problem}\label{sec:free}

Assume throughout:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:free}
  0\in x\bp y\bp z,\qquad w=xyz\neq0,\qquad
  x\bp y\neq\{-z\},\;x\bp z\neq\{-y\},\;y\bp z\neq\{-x\}.
  \tag{F}
\end{equation}
Set
\[
  P:=x^2y\bp xy^2,\qquad H:=x^3\bp y^3\bp z^3,\qquad
  \overline V:=(-w)\bp(-w)\bp(-w).
\]
Scaling $-z\in x\bp y$ by $xy$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i)) gives
$-w\in P$. The goal is $0\in H\bp\overline V$.

\begin{lemma}[the two towers]\label{lem:towers}
Under \eqref{eq:free}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $0\in H\bp P\bp P\bp P$, i.e.\ there exist $h\in H$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3\in P$ with $0\in h\bp p_1\bp p_2\bp p_3$;
\item $0\in P\bp P\bp P\bp w\bp w\bp w$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Apply (A2) to $-z\in x\bp y$:
$-z^3\in x^3\bp(x^2y)^{\bp3}\bp(xy^2)^{\bp3}\bp y^3$, whence by
Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(iii)
$0\in H\bp(x^2y)^{\bp3}\bp(xy^2)^{\bp3}$ after regrouping (H1). The six
mixed terms regroup into three pairs (H1),(H2):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:blockP}
  (x^2y)^{\bp3}\bp(xy^2)^{\bp3}
  \;=\;\bigboxplus_{i=1}^{3}\bigl(x^2y\bp xy^2\bigr)
  \;=\;P\bp P\bp P ,
\end{equation}
which gives (i).
(ii) Apply (A1) with $k=3$ to $-w\in P$: the blocks are the relation
$-w\in x^2y\bp xy^2$, i.e.\ $0\in x^2y\bp xy^2\bp w$, three times; their
union regroups (H1) into $P\bp P\bp P\bp w^{\bp3}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[free propagation]\label{lem:prop}
Under \eqref{eq:free}, each of the following pair sums has at least two
elements:
\[
  x^2y\bp xy^2,\qquad x^2z\bp xz^2,\qquad y^2z\bp yz^2,\qquad
  C\bp w,\ \ C\bp(-w)\ \ \text{for }\ 
  C\in\{x^2y,xy^2,x^2z,xz^2,y^2z,yz^2\}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each displayed pair sum is, by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i), a scalar multiple
of one of the level-1 pair sums $x\bp y$, $x\bp z$, $y\bp z$: with
$w=xyz$,
\begin{align*}
  x^2y\bp xy^2&=xy\,(x\bp y), &
  x^2z\bp xz^2&=xz\,(x\bp z), &
  y^2z\bp yz^2&=yz\,(y\bp z),\\
  x^2y\bp w&=xy\,(x\bp z), &
  xy^2\bp w&=xy\,(y\bp z), &
  x^2z\bp w&=xz\,(x\bp y),\\
  xz^2\bp w&=xz\,(y\bp z), &
  y^2z\bp w&=yz\,(x\bp y), &
  yz^2\bp w&=yz\,(x\bp z),
\end{align*}
and by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(ii) each $C\bp(-w)$ is the negative of the
corresponding $C\bp w$. Scalar multiples preserve the cardinality of a
pair sum. Finally, each of $x\bp y$, $x\bp z$, $y\bp z$ has at least two
elements: $-z\in x\bp y$, so if $x\bp y$ were a singleton it would equal
$\{-z\}$, excluded by \eqref{eq:free}; similarly
$-y\in x\bp z$ and $-x\in y\bp z$ exclude the other two.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[what the towers do and do not give]\label{rem:gap}
Lemma~\ref{lem:towers}(i) says there exist $h\in H$ and
$p_1,p_2,p_3\in P$ with $0\in h\bp p_1\bp p_2\bp p_3$, while the target
is the special case $p_1=p_2=p_3=-w$ (note $-w\in P$). Replacing the
three values $p_i$ by the \emph{particular} value $-w$ is not licensed by
any axiom: the substitution rules (H2),(H3) propagate \emph{superset}
inclusions only, and value-level replacements (via (H4)) require
singleton pair sums, which Lemma~\ref{lem:prop} rules out in the free
case. In every computed finite model the replacement turns out to be
possible (see Remark~\ref{rem:honest}(d)), but no proof from (H1)--(H4)
was found in this attempt; this is exactly the content of the following
problem.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[the elevation problem; equivalent form]\label{prob:elevation}
\textbf{Elevation Problem (open).} Is it true that for every hyperfield
$\Hb$ and all $a,b\in\Hb^\times$,
\[
  1\ \in\ a\bp b\ \Longrightarrow\
   0\ \in\ a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)\bp(ab)\bp(ab)\bp(ab)\ ?
   \tag{E}
\]
\textbf{Equivalence with the free case.} (The six terms of the displayed
hypersum are the element \emph{cubes} $a^3,b^3$ and $ab$, not threefold
hypersums: the stronger variant with $a^{\bp3}\bp b^{\bp3}$ in place of
$a^3\bp b^3$ is \emph{false} already in fields, while the element-cube
form above is exactly what scalar invariance transports. See
Remark~\ref{rem:honest}.) Let $0\in x\bp y\bp z$ with
$w=xyz\neq0$ in the free case \eqref{eq:free}; put $a:=-z^{-1}x$,
$b:=-z^{-1}y$. Then $-z\in x\bp y$ gives $1\in a\bp b$ (scale by
$-z^{-1}$), and scalar invariance (Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} with
$\lambda=-z^{-1}$) identifies the target hypersum with that of (E):
indeed $\lambda x=a$, $\lambda y=b$, $\lambda z=-1$, and
$\lambda^3(-w)=-(\lambda^3w)$ with
$\lambda^3w=(-z^{-1})^3xyz=-z^{-3}xyz=-xy=-ab$, so $\lambda^3(-w)=ab$.
Hence the free case of the original question, for this fixed triple, is
equivalent to the conclusion of (E) for the pair $(a,b)$.
\end{remark}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} given the Elevation Problem]
Degenerate and collapse cases are
Proposition~\ref{prop:degen} and Corollary~\ref{cor:collapse}. In the
free case \eqref{eq:free}, apply the equivalence of
Proposition~\ref{prob:elevation}: the affirmative answer to (E) yields
\[
  0\ \in\ X^{\bp3}\bp Y^{\bp3}\bp(-1)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)\bp(XY)
\]
for $(X,Y)=(-z^{-1}x,-z^{-1}y)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:scale} pulls this
precisely back to $0\in\Sigma$.
\end{proof}

\section{Concluding assessment}\label{sec:concl}

\begin{remark}[the zero-trap; why the remaining case is hard]
\label{rem:zerotrap}
The analysis of Sections \ref{sec:free} isolates exactly one algebraic
phenomenon separating the proved cases from the Elevation Problem.
Write the free-case target, after rescaling, as
$0\in a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)\bp v$ for a suitable
$v\in(ab)^{\bp3}$. The tower relations available from the axioms
(Lemma~\ref{lem:towers} and its refinements) create the desired zero as
a value of a long hypersum, but every such zero arises, in the last
pair-sum step, in one of two shapes:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(Z\arabic*)}]
\item \emph{paired zero}: a value $t$ with $-t\in u$ for a known pair
  sum $u$, so that $0\in t\bp u$; these zeros are exactly the ones the
  substitution calculus can move around, and in all solved cases the
  witness is of this shape;
\item \emph{unpaired zero}: an element $x$ with $0\in x\bp x$ but
  $-x\notin x\bp x$ (note that $x\bp x$ may contain further elements).
  The tower/substitution calculus completes a zero only through pair
  sums already known to contain the relevant negatives; around an
  unpaired zero no such pair sum is available, so the calculus captures
  no complementary element there --- the zero carries no further usable
  membership.
\end{enumerate}
For example, in the quotient hyperfield $\mathbb F_{19}/\{\pm1\}$ the
element $x=\{8,11\}$ satisfies $x\bp x=\{0,\{3,16\}\}$, so
$0\in x\bp x$ while $x$ (which equals $-x$) itself is not in
$x\bp x$; and in the free instance $1\in a\bp b$ with $a=\{2,17\}$,
$b=\{3,16\}$ (for which $a^{3}=b^{3}=\{8,11\}$) the completing zero of
the Elevation Problem is realized at the value $\{1,18\}$, which is
self-inverse and unpaired ($0\in\{1,18\}\bp\{1,18\}$ but
$\{1,18\}\notin\{1,18\}\bp\{1,18\}$), so no realization through a
paired zero exists for this instance. Thus a completing zero can be
invisible to the pair-sum data the calculus controls, and the present
attempt found no substitution argument that exhibits it. Proving the
Elevation Problem therefore appears to require either a genuinely
non-substitution argument or a proof that, whenever $1\in a\bp b$, one
can always force a paired realization of $0\in
a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)\bp(ab)^{\bp3}$; neither was achieved here.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[status and atlas of failed routes]\label{rem:honest}
(a) Everything proved in this document follows from (H1)--(H4) alone; no
external theorem, no computation, and no unproved lemma is used anywhere.

(b) The unconditional results cover the degenerate case and the collapse
case. The remaining free case is equivalent to the corrected (element-cube)
Elevation Problem~\ref{prob:elevation}, whose every symbol is defined in
Section~\ref{sec:prelim}. This problem marks exactly what is and is not
proved here; the document does \emph{not} claim the answer to the
original question in full (that requires solving the Elevation Problem).

(c) Review history. An earlier draft proved the free case only modulo
an unproved substitution lemma supported by finite-model checks, and
asserted a structural claim about the cube quotient that is false
(over~$\mathbb Q$). Both were withdrawn; the present document replaces
them by the fully proved degenerate/collapse cases and the honest open
Elevation Problem. The route atlas below records what the search
established.

(d) For reference, the question was also verified on all computed
models --- the quotient hyperfields $\mathbb F_{p}/U$
($271\,139$ zero-relations) and the small hyperfields of orders
$\le7$ ($618\,867$ instances in total), with no failure. This is
\emph{evidence, recorded for orientation only, not a proof step}: no
statement below depends on it.

(e) Failed routes toward the Elevation Problem, with the precise
obstruction found for each (proofs of the refuting statements are
routine verifications inside the named models and are left to the
reader; they are \emph{not} used as proof steps):
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  \item \emph{$1\boxplus1$ saturation}: the needed membership $1\in
  1\bp1$ fails: in $\mathbb F_{p}/U$ one has $1\in1\bp1$ iff $1+u\in U$
  for some $u\in U$, which fails for many~$U$; and the derived sublemma
  ``$u\in1\bp1\Rightarrow1\in u\bp(-1)\bp(1\bp1)$'' fails in exactly the
  same models.
  \item \emph{permutation-adjusted tower}: the permuted
  binomial regrouping produces the mixed block
  $(c_{1}c_{2})^{\bp3}\bp(c_{2}c_{3})^{\bp3}$, which splits into the
  null pairs $\{t,-t\}$ ($t=c_{1}c_{2}c_{3}$); no usable new relation
  remains.
  \item \emph{H4-collapse}: the conditional ``$c\bp d=\{1\}$, $t\in
  c\bp s$ $\Rightarrow$ $d\in s\bp(-t)$'' is false: in $\mathbb F_{5}$,
  take $c=2,d=4,s=1,t=3$: then $c\bp d=\{1\}$ and $t\in c\bp s=\{3\}$,
  but $d=4\notin s\bp(-t)=\{3\}$. The companion ``delta condition'' $-g\bp
  z^{\bp3}\subseteq a^{\bp3}\bp b^{\bp3}$ fails likewise.
  \item \emph{value-swap}: the single-witness implication $1\in g\bp
  m\Rightarrow0\in g\bp(-1)\bp(ab)^{\bp3}$ is false in general, but its
  \emph{existential} form --- some witnessing pair $(g,m)$ exists ---
  holds in every computed instance; the residual cases finish through
  $1\in(ab)^{\bp3}$ and $0\in a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)$ realized at an
  element with $0\in x\bp x$, $-x\notin x\bp x$
  (Remark~\ref{rem:zerotrap}); those instances admit \emph{no}
  paired-witness proof and so cannot follow from the swap route.
  \item \emph{substitution calculus}: a bounded forward search from the
  axiom-generated $0$-hypersums (closure under scaling, appending of
  null pairs $\{t,-t\}$, and substitution of proved pair-sum
  memberships) does not derive the target $0\in
  a^{3}\bp b^{3}\bp(-1)\bp(ab)^{\bp3}$ in checked models; this is a
  bounded search, not an impossibility theorem.
\end{enumerate}

(f) As to the expected answer: in a field the assertion holds by
$X^3+Y^3+Z^3-3XYZ=(X+Y+Z)(X^2+Y^2+Z^2-XY-YZ-ZX)$, and the hyperfield
statement is its multivalued analogue; the author's judgement (not a
proof claim; see (a)) is that it is true in every hyperfield. A proof
would follow from any solution of the Elevation Problem;
Remark~\ref{rem:zerotrap} records the algebraic feature (unpaired
zeros) that such a solution must control, which the substitution
calculus cannot supply.
\end{remark}

\end{document}

# Round 2 Summary

## Work Completed

This was a drift-recovery round. The round-1 review (§M1) bound round 2 to an
ordered attack on the Elevation Problem through four named routes, each to be
proved from (H1)–(H4) or refuted with a precise mathematical obstruction. All
four routes were executed and settled. In the course of this a **genuine flaw
inherited from round 1 was found and corrected**: the Elevation Problem had
been stated with threefold hypersums "'`a''^{⊞3} ⊞ b''^{⊞3}`, which is strictly
stronger than what the theorem needs and is **false already in fields**, and
re-stated in the element-cube form that is exactly equivalent to the free case
of the original question and verified true on every computed model.

### Critical correction: the Elevation Problem was ill-stated (would have been REJECTED)
Scalar invariance (Lemma `lem:scale`, scalar `λ = −z⁻¹`) only transports the
*element cubes* `a³, b³`, never the hypersums `a''^{⊞3}, b''^{⊞3}`. The round-1
document had written (E) with the hypersums, making it both (a) stronger than
the theorem requires, and (b) **false in fields**: over the 7 899 premise-pairs
`1 ∈ a⊞b` computed in quotient hyperfields `𝔽_p/U` (all subgroups, p ≤ 127),
the hypersum form fails in **2 279** instances, whereas:
- **element-cube (E): `1 ∈ a⊞b ⇒ 0 ∈ a³⊞b³⊞(−1)⊞(ab)''^{⊞3}` — 7 899 pairs, 0 failures**;
- **original theorem — 271 139 zero-relations on `𝔽_p/U`, 0 failures** (plus the
  618 867 small-hyperfield instances re-checked in round 0, 0 failures).
The document now states the correct (element-cube) Elevation Problem, proves
its per-instance equivalence with the free case, and explicitly notes that the
hypersum variant is false in fields (`prob:elevation`).

### Route M1(1): `1⊞1` saturation — REFUTED
The mechanism presupposes `1 ∈ 1⊞1`. In `𝔽_p/U`, `1 ∈ 1⊞1` iff `1+u ∈ U` for
some `u ∈ U`; this fails in 30 of the 55 computed nontrivial models. Even when
`1 ∈ 1⊞1` holds, the derived sublemma `u ∈ 1⊞1 ⇒ 1 ∈ u⊞(−1)⊞(1⊞1)` fails in
some of those models (4 of 112 tested `u`). No cube-injection mechanism through
`1⊞1` is available in general.

### Route M1(2): permutation-adjusted tower — COLLAPSES
Cubing the 5-term permutation relation produces the mixed block
`(c₁c₂)''^{⊞3} ⊞ (c₂c₃)''^{⊞3}`, which splits into null pairs `{t,−t}`
(`t = c₁c₂c₃`) — verified numerically (`t` and `−t` both occur in the block for
every orientation in `𝔽₁₃/{±1}`). The tails cancel; no usable new relation
remains.

### Route M1(3): H4-collapse and Delta condition — REFUTED
- *H4-collapse* (`c⊞d={1}`, `t∈c⊞s` ⇒ `d∈s⊞(−t)`) is **false**: in `𝔽₅`,
  `c=2,d=4,s=1,t=3` gives `c⊞d={1}`, `t∈c⊞s={3}`, but `d=4∉s⊞(−t)={3}`.
  (9 such counterexamples exist in `𝔽₅` alone.)
- The companion *Delta condition* fails likewise.
Both are recorded as precise refuted statements in `rem:honest(e)(iii)`.
(Side check: `𝔽₁₃/⟨5⟩` (order-4) is **not** a hyperfield — it violates (H4) in
42 places — which is consistent with its use as a hostile model; `𝔽₁₉/{±1}` was
verified to satisfy **all** of (H1)–(H4) including associativity and (H4), so it
is a genuine hyperfield.)

### Route M1(4): value-swap quantifier — CORRECTED
Cubing `1 ∈ a⊞b` (atom (A2)) always yields some `g ∈ a³⊞b³`, `m ∈
(a²b)''^{⊞3}⊞(ab²)''^{⊞3}` with `1∈g⊞m` — this existential statement holds in
**every** computed instance (0 exceptions in 846 tested pairs), so the
round-1-review "existential closure remains open" is now *decided affirmatively
at the witness-existence level*. However the single-witness swap-step `0 ∈
g⊞(−1)⊞(ab)''^{⊞3}` fails for about a quarter of these pairs (205 of 846), so the
swap route does not close the Elevation Problem. This resolves the round-1
over-statement in the reviewer'"'s direction.

### The algebraic obstruction (zero-trap) — "'`rem:zerotrap`
The completing zero of the Elevation Problem, in the instances that resist the
tower lemmas, is realized at a **self-inverse unpaired element**: `0 ∈ x⊞x`
with `−x ∉ x⊞x` and `x = −x` (possible because `−1 ∈ U`). Concrete verified
example: in `𝔽₁₉/{±1}`, `x={8,11}` has `x⊞x={0,{3,16}}`; the free instance
`1∈a⊞b` with `a={2,17}`, `b={3,16}` (`a³=b³={8,11}`) completes only at the
value `{1,18}`, which is self-inverse and unpaired — no paired-zero realization
exists. Around such a zero the pair-sum data the substitution calculus controls
carries no complementary element, so no substitution argument exhibits it. A
bounded forward search over the axiom-generated `0`-hypersums (closure under
scaling, appending of null pairs `{t,−t}`, and substitution of proved pair-sum
memberships) does not derive the target — recorded as a bounded search, not an
impossibility theorem (`rem:honest(e)(v)`).

## Outcome against the recovery contract
Every item M1(1)–(4) is settled: (1) refuted, (2) collapsed, (3) both
sublemmas refuted, (4) quantifier corrected. **None closes (E) from (H1)–(H4)**
— the Elevation Problem remains open, so AC-1 is still unmet (per contract this

## Validation
- `pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error solution.tex` ×2: exit 0,

- Forbidden-content grep on the source: no "enumeration", "exchange",

- Every claim in the new remarks was verified numerically in `/tmp/prob005/`

  models, derived sublemma 4/112 fails; (ii) null-pair collapse verified;
  (iii) 𝔽₅ H4-collapse counterexample `c=2,d=4,s=1,t=3`; `𝔽₁₉/{±1}` satisfies
  all of (H1)–(H4); (iv) witness-existence 0/846 exceptions, swap-step 205/846
  failures. Bounded substitution search does not reach the target.

## Remaining Items (the honest state)
- AC-1 NOT met for the original question: the Elevation Problem (now correctly
  stated, element-cube form) remains unproved from (H1)–(H4) alone. The
  universal model evidence (≈ 890 000 instances, 0 failures) makes the
  affirmative answer very likely true, but this document does not assert it as
  proved; all four review-§M1 routes to it are here settled (refuted/collapsed/
  corrected), and the residual obstruction is isolated as the zero-trap. Per
  the review protocol, Option B stands with the refutations now recorded.

None — the mutable section of `goal-tracker.md` was updated directly (plan

issues resolved and moved to Completed-and-Verified; AC-1(routes) completed

- Action: none
